name: TG (tidwall geometry library)
workload: Point-in-polygon on 10K random points against Brazil polygon (39,914 points) and other polygons, best of 10 runs
claimed_speedup: Brazil: tg/ystripes 15,174,761 ops/s and tg/natural 10,143,419 ops/s vs geos/prepared 7,885,512 ops/s and geos/none 29,708 ops/s; Texas: 22,453,447 vs 9,868,950 (prepared)
tradeoffs: Not a full GIS library (no convex hull, voronoi etc.); single tg.c file; indexed polygons use more memory and build time (ystripes ~884us vs GEOS prepared ~2060us for Brazil).
caveats: Own benchmark by author; geometry predicates only (PIP, intersects, parsing), not GEOS's wider algorithms. Found as repo with benchmark, not a paper.
found_via: WebSearch 'arXiv point-in-polygon OR spatial join GPU OR SIMD faster than GEOS code available github' -> tidwall/fast-spatial-joins/tg; github.com/tidwall/tg and docs/BENCHMARKS.md

name: HXT parallel 3D Delaunay (in Gmsh)
workload: 3D Delaunay triangulation of 1M to 100M+ random points, sequential and parallel
claimed_speedup: about 3x faster than CGAL 4.12 sequentially for 1 million points; 4.48 s for 10 million points on a 64-core Xeon Phi; CGAL could not do 100M points in tested time; 3 billion tetrahedra in 53 s on AMD EPYC
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700HQ; Intel Xeon Phi 7210 (64 cores); AMD EPYC 7551 dual socket
stars_or_usage: 127 stars on GitHub mirror; Gmsh is widely used FEM mesher
tradeoffs: GPL (with linking exception for external libraries) code inside a large mesh generator; HXT lives under contrib/hxt in Gmsh; floating-point predicates are exact-adaptive.
caveats: Compiler and flags not read (arXiv HTML fetch was rate-limited, abstract page only); repo_url is the live-clones mirror of the canonical gitlab.onelab.info/gmsh/gmsh (gitlab was blocked); the paper is 2018 so CGAL 4.12 is old; last_commit is for Gmsh as a whole.
found_via: WebSearch 'arXiv Delaunay triangulation open source implementation faster than CGAL speedup github C++'

name: gDel3D
workload: 3D Delaunay triangulation of real-world models and synthetic point sets on GPU+CPU hybrid
claimed_speedup: 6-9x speedup over sequential CGAL on real-world models, up to 10x on synthetic uniform distributions (paper); project page: up to 10x over CGAL 3D Delaunay
tradeoffs: Requires an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA); hybrid GPU insertion/flipping then CPU star splaying; repo is a mirror of NUS code.
caveats: I3D 2014 paper, CGAL 4.2 is very old; compiler flags not stated; paper URL is a third-party copy (codeyarns.com), project page https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~tants/gdel3d.html states up to 10x vs CGAL; repo license read from GitHub summary.
found_via: WebSearch 'Geogram Delaunay triangulation parallel faster than CGAL' and 'arXiv Delaunay ... faster than CGAL'; github.com/ashwin/gDel3D

name: GeoToolbox KdBoxTree
workload: Bulk load, range queries and nearest queries on points/boxes from 10^2 to 10^6 elements on ESRI shapefile datasets and a synthetic uniform set
claimed_speedup: KdBoxTree is quickest to bulk-load and fastest at range queries on box keys, and on point keys from 10^4 elements; Boost R-tree lags behind in query performance; others 2-4x slower builds (no single ratio vs Boost given in README text read)
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2026 and Clang 22 on Windows (flags not stated)
hardware: ASUS ROG Strix G16 laptop, Windows 11 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: KdBoxTree has no dynamic insert/erase; Boost R*-tree is the most versatile; memory is higher than nanoflann.
caveats: First-party benchmark; CPU model missing; results are in a separate repo (ikolev21/ikolev21.github.io) that I did not open. Same README also compares GEOS STRtree, nanoflann and tidwall rtree (GEOS faster on Polygon dataset box queries, tidwall on 2D sets 10^4-10^5). Last commit date came from a page summary.
found_via: WebSearch 'spatial index R-tree paper faster than Boost.Geometry GEOS open source C++'

name: tidwall rtree.c
workload: Insert/erase/reinsert and box queries on evenly spread datasets (per GeoToolbox third-party comparison)
claimed_speedup: Per GeoToolbox README: 'faster than Boost at insert/erase/reinsert and at querying afterwards'; own README: 1M points inserted at 151.3 ns/op random order, searched at 242.4 ns/op, no Boost comparison
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2026 / Clang 22 (GeoToolbox); own README flags not read
hardware: ASUS ROG Strix G16 (GeoToolbox); AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (own README)
tradeoffs: No bulk loading; builds by insertion so sensitive to insertion order; dimensions and scalar type fixed at compile time.
caveats: Evidence is a qualitative sentence in a third-party (but small, 0-star) comparison without numbers on the page I read; own README has no Boost comparison.
found_via: GeoToolbox README (found via 'spatial index R-tree paper faster than Boost.Geometry GEOS open source C++')

name: nanoflann
baseline: FLANN kd-tree (also compared by GeoToolbox against Boost.Geometry R*-tree)
workload: kd-tree build and nearest-neighbour queries on 100K uniform points and ~150K real scan points
claimed_speedup: ~50% time saving with respect to the original FLANN implementation; GeoToolbox: faster than KdBoxTree on point proximity queries up to 10^5 elements and lowest memory
tradeoffs: Points only (boxes need 2N-dim embedding costing ~2x); no insert/erase of arbitrary elements; stores indexes into caller's dataset.
caveats: Baseline FLANN is not in the category list; README numbers are graphs without stated CPU/compiler; license shown as 'BSD' on page (SPDX BSD-2-Clause is my reading, unconfirmed); latest release v1.10.1 June 2026, exact last commit not read; Boost comparison comes only from the GeoToolbox README.
found_via: GeoToolbox README and WebSearch 'header-only C++ R-tree OR kd-tree OR BVH library benchmark faster than Boost.Geometry'

name: MeshLib
workload: Mesh boolean operations on a 2M-triangle Nefertiti model, a 280K-triangle dental scan and simple edge-case objects, min of 10 iterations, I/O excluded
claimed_speedup: 47x faster than CGAL and 2.9x faster than Manifold on Nefertiti; 153x faster than Blender boolean
hardware: Apple M5 MacBook Air (10-core CPU, 32GB), macOS 26
tradeoffs: Source-available: free for non-commercial and educational use, commercial use needs a licence; CGAL compared uses exact arithmetic (slower but exact) while MeshLib uses robust floating point.
caveats: Vendor blog from the company selling the product; compiler and flags not stated; repo says method, data and input meshes are public but I did not open them. Non-OSI license so code must not be copied. Last commit date not read.
found_via: WebSearch 'convex hull OR mesh boolean OR winding number library paper faster than CGAL open source C++ github'
